newsitem.title: USA: U.S. airports cope with growth in aviation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. airports cope with growth in aviation.

text.p: Federal aviation officials say the biggest drag on aviation growth in the United States is the shortage of airport capacity, and no new airports are set to be built any time soon.
But airports are finding ways to cope.
The foes of new airports are the NIMBYs -- opponents who will support growth, but "Not In My Back Yard," Federal Aviation Administrator David Hinson said this week.

One way airport authorities will meet expected passenger surges is by expanding existing facilities. There is also new technology to better utilize airspace and abandoned military airfields are being converted to civilian use.
The larger jets now flying also allow airports to handle more passengers without more runways and terminals.
Hinson said in remarks at the National Press Club that "the single, biggest constraint to the continued successful development of commercial aviation in the United States is airport capacity."
He said a shortage of air traffic controllers could be remedied, airlines could handle the growth and new pilots could be hired, but, "We don't have enough concrete. We don't have enough gates."
U.S. airports now handle about 500 million passengers a year and the FAA estimated they would have to cope with double that number by 2010.

Specialists agree that the new Denver airport opened last year was the last in the foreseeable future, due not only to its $4.9 billion cost, but also to a scarcity of "greenfield" sites near cities as well as to environmental opposition.
However, even without any new airports to cope with a surge of passengers, an airports association official said, "I'm confident we will be able to handle them."
Richard Marchi, senior vice president of Airports Council International of North America, said existing airports could be expanded both on the outside and inside.
The outside expansion, he said, included new runways, new spacing and weather forecasting methods that permitted more aircraft to land and take off in the allotted airspace.
Marchi said "the new spacing system will allow planes to fly closer together safely, enabling airports to handle more planes in a more orderly fashion."
FAA officials added that new instrument landing systems would allow planes to operate with reduced visibility, thus avoiding delays in bad weather and then "bunching" when the weather cleared.
Marchi said additional capacity was being found at military bases being shut down and at downsized Air National Guard and air reserve bases located on municipal airports.

He said Austin, Texas, had taken over the nearby abandoned Bergstrom Air Force Base and, in one of the largest of the swords-to-plowshares conversions, was turning it into its new city airport expected to begin operations this year.
Pease Air Force Base in New Hampshire has already been converted into the new Portsmouth, N.H., airport.
But most of the time, Marchi said, airports were expanding their existing facilities with major improvements either underway or planned for nearly all major U.S. airports.
The cost of new runways and runway extensions being built was estimated at more than $6 billion, the FAA said.
